title: Insist on yourself
last: GIVE MY OWN INNER GLEAM A FAIR HEARING.

cards: Music teachers meet this student now and then. They love one guitarist so much that they learn every lick, every bend, every bit of attitude. And they get good.
Really good. Close your eyes and it almost sounds like the real thing. Almost.
Then one day the teacher asks them to play something of their own, and the room goes quiet. They've spent years becoming a very good copy.
Emerson has a sentence for that student, short enough to write on the back of a hand: insist on yourself; never imitate.

teach.b: First, the line, from Self-Reliance: "Insist on yourself; never imitate." Two commands, one positive, one negative, the same command seen from two sides. Second, his reason.
Your own gift, Emerson says, you can offer at any moment with the force of a whole lifetime's cultivation behind it.
A talent borrowed from someone else, you only half own. You have to reach for it every time, and it's never quite there. The copy can be good.
It just can't grow, because its roots are in someone else's life. Third, the great names.

Who could have taught Shakespeare to be Shakespeare? Nobody, Emerson says, and no amount of studying him will make another one. In Emerson's telling, the great names he admires got there by doing what only they could do.
So the way to honor someone you admire isn't to become them. It's to do with your life what they did with theirs. Fourth, a word about envy.

Earlier in the same essay, Emerson writes that a person reaches a point where they're convinced that "envy is ignorance": not knowing your own portion. Wanting someone else's gift is a way of not looking at yours.
None of this means don't learn from anyone. The guitar student should learn the licks; Emerson himself, in The American Scholar, called books the best of things, well used.
The question is what happens next: do the borrowed things become a ladder to your own voice, or a costume you never take off?

how: Some readers take 'insist on yourself; never imitate' as permission to learn from others while refusing to become a copy of them, letting what they borrow lead toward their own voice.

o: Emerson's call to grow your own gift, not copy another's
a rule to never learn from teachers or great books
a demand that others agree with you and give in

games.q: inside insist on yourself: tap the pairs.

s: Emerson says never learn from anyone
he called books the best of things, well used. the question is whether what you borrow becomes a ladder or a costume.
Emerson says a borrowed talent is only half owned
your own gift has a whole lifetime of cultivation behind it.
Emerson says studying Shakespeare will make another Shakespeare
he asks who could have taught Shakespeare, and the answer is nobody.

games.q: you admire one artist so much that you can copy them perfectly. what does Emerson's essay point you toward?
o: keep copying until you're as good as they are.
use what you learned to find what only you can do.
stop learning from anyone at all.
games.why: "insist on yourself; never imitate." the way to honor them is to do with your life what they did with theirs.

practice: Bring to mind something ordinary you do every day: how you make coffee, write an email, greet people, or pray, if you pray. Ask quietly whose way it is, and whether you chose it or copied it from someone without noticing.
There's no need to change anything; just find one small place where your own way is waiting under a borrowed one.

wordCard.voice: Insist on yourself. Emerson's line from Self-Reliance: your own gift carries a lifetime behind it, and a borrowed one you only half own. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: never imitate. Your own way may come out a little clumsy at first. Until tomorrow.
